tagline: Gulf Drive links island beaches with a history of rebuilt crossings.
intro: Gulf Drive runs north from Longboat Pass onto Anna Maria Island, where the beach lies immediately west of the road in Bradenton Beach. This stretch of State Road 789 became the Bradenton Beach Scenic Highway on April 17, 2001. Florida Scenic Highways describes a landscaped waterfront corridor for walking and biking, with beaches, picnic areas and boat ramps along the way. Its designation covers Gulf Drive through the city, from the Longboat Pass Bridge to the northern city limits.

The connection across Longboat Pass first opened in 1926, but the wooden bridge was damaged that year and swept away in 1932. A replacement restored the link to Longboat Key in 1957. That same year, a concrete bridge replaced the wooden crossing from Cortez on the mainland, giving Bradenton Beach another renewed road connection. By the completion of the Longboat Pass replacement, the road from St. Armands Circle to the north end of Anna Maria Island had been renumbered as a segment of State Road 789.

Start at Longboat Pass and follow Gulf Drive South through trees into the town’s resort homes and businesses. At the junction with State Road 684, the road becomes Gulf Drive North. Continue past more resort development toward the northern city boundary and neighboring Holmes Beach.

moments.title: Longboat Pass
moments.text: The bridge at Longboat Pass restores a connection that was absent for twenty-five years. A county bond financed the first wooden link between Bradenton Beach and Longboat Key in 1926. It opened in August, suffered hurricane damage in October and was swept away during a high tide in March 1932. The replacement arrived in 1957. The present crossing carries State Road 789 over the pass; on the Anna Maria Island side, the road takes the name Gulf Drive South. The earlier crossing used a swing bridge; the route description identifies the present crossing as a drawbridge.

moments.title: Bradenton Beach
moments.text: An elephant led the parade when Bradenton Beach demonstrated the strength of its new concrete bridge from Cortez in 1957. The crossing replaced a wooden bridge, answering residents’ wish for a stronger link to the mainland. It remained a toll bridge until 1964 to help recover its cost. The community had been settled in 1893, taking its earlier name from neighboring Cortez across the water. The town’s name also reflects its mainland ties: during the 1920s land boom, developers used Bradenton Beach instead of Cortez Beach to suggest greater proximity to Bradenton.

moments.title: Wreck of the Regina
moments.text: The Regina carried molasses when it sank on a sandbar off Bradenton Beach on March 8, 1940. Its cargo exceeded 350,000 gallons, and eight crew members were aboard the tanker barge when it sank. Built in Belfast in 1904, the tanker was under tow by Minima when the towline broke near Egmont Key. Both vessels had been trying to reach shelter in Tampa Bay. The cook died while attempting to leave the vessel; the other seven crew members were rescued. In April 2005, the wreck became Florida’s tenth Underwater Archaeological Preserve.
